title: The Water We Cannot See
text:
When people think of water shortages, they usually picture dry riverbeds and shrinking reservoirs. Much of the world’s fresh water, however, lies out of sight, stored underground in layers of sand, gravel and porous rock known as aquifers. This groundwater sustains wells, springs and the flow of many rivers in the dry season, and in large farming regions it supplies much of the water used for irrigation.

Groundwater has obvious attractions. It is available close to where it is needed, it is often cleaner than surface water, and a farmer with a pump can draw on it whenever the crop requires, without waiting for a canal to deliver its share. These advantages have transformed agriculture in many dry areas. The difficulty is that aquifers are replenished slowly, mainly by rain and river water seeping down through the soil, and in many places water is now being pumped out far faster than it is returned.

The consequences of this imbalance accumulate quietly. Water tables fall, so that wells must be dug deeper and pumps must work harder, raising costs for farmers and favouring those who can afford the most powerful equipment. In coastal areas, excessive pumping can draw seawater into aquifers and make the water salty. In some cities the ground itself has sunk as underground layers are drained and compacted. Because none of this is visible in the way a dry river is visible, it often goes unnoticed until the damage is severe.

Managing groundwater is difficult precisely because it is shared and hidden. One farmer’s restraint benefits all his neighbours, while his own pumping costs him little in the short run. Measuring how much water is taken, pricing electricity for pumps sensibly, recharging aquifers by capturing rainwater and encouraging crops and methods that use less water are among the measures that can help. The first step, however, is to recognise that an invisible resource is not an inexhaustible one.

title: Sleep and the Remembering Mind
text:
Sleep was once regarded as little more than a pause, a nightly interruption of useful activity during which the body rested and the mind switched off. Research over recent decades has overturned that picture. The sleeping brain is far from idle, and among its most important activities appears to be the strengthening of memories formed during the day.

When we learn something new, whether a list of words, a route through an unfamiliar town or a piece of music, the memory is at first fragile and easily disturbed. Studies suggest that during sleep the brain revisits recent experiences, reinforcing some connections and allowing others to fade. People who sleep after learning a task often perform it better the next day than those who have spent the same number of hours awake, and they seem better able to draw general patterns from particular examples.

The implications for students are uncomfortable. The familiar practice of staying up all night before an examination may feel productive, but it deprives the brain of precisely the process that helps to fix what has been studied. A tired student also finds it harder to concentrate, so that the extra hours yield less than they appear to. Learning spread over several days, with adequate sleep between sessions, is likely to produce more durable results than the same amount of study crammed into a single sleepless night.

None of this means that sleep is a substitute for effort. The brain can only consolidate what has been learned in the first place, and a night’s rest will not supply knowledge that was never acquired. But it does suggest that sleep deserves a place in our thinking about learning, not as an indulgence to be sacrificed when work presses, but as part of the work itself.

title: The Changing Household
text:
In much of South Asia, the extended family household, in which grandparents, parents, children and sometimes uncles and their families share one roof, has long been regarded as the natural form of domestic life. It pooled incomes, divided labour, cared for the young and the old, and passed on customs from one generation to the next. Today that arrangement is under visible strain, and the reasons lie less in changing values than in changing circumstances.

The most powerful force is migration. As young people move to cities, or abroad, in search of education and work, they leave behind households that are thinner in the middle, with the elderly and the very young remaining in the village. In the city, small flats and high rents make it difficult to accommodate a large family even where there is a wish to do so. Women’s growing participation in paid work, meanwhile, has altered the division of labour on which the old household depended.

It would be wrong to conclude that family ties have weakened in proportion. Many migrants send a large part of their earnings home, return for weddings and festivals, and speak to their parents far more often than distance once allowed. The family, in other words, is being reorganised rather than dissolved; it is becoming a network spread across places rather than a single household under one roof.

This reorganisation nonetheless raises difficult questions for public policy. The extended household was, among other things, an informal welfare system, providing care in old age and support in illness without any help from the state. As fewer elderly people live with their children, the need for pensions, accessible health care and community services is likely to grow. Societies that have relied on the family to do this work will have to decide how much of it the state should now share.

title: The Limits of Tolerance
text:
Tolerance is among the most praised virtues of modern public life, yet it is less often examined than praised. To tolerate something is not to approve of it. We do not tolerate what we like; we enjoy it. Tolerance begins only where there is disapproval, and consists in the decision not to suppress what we disapprove of, even though we might have the power to do so. It is, in this sense, a discipline imposed on our own reactions.

Why should we accept such a discipline? One reason is humility. History offers many examples of opinions confidently held by the majority of one age that later came to be regarded as mistaken. A person aware of this may hesitate before silencing views he believes to be false. A second reason is respect for persons: adults are entitled to reach their own conclusions about how to live, and to be treated as capable of doing so, even when they choose in ways others regret. A third is prudential. Societies that attempt to impose uniformity usually purchase peace at the price of resentment, and the peace does not last.

Tolerance, however, cannot be unlimited. A society that tolerated every act, including violence against those who are themselves peaceful, would not be tolerant but defenceless, and would soon find that the intolerant had abolished tolerance altogether. The difficult question is therefore not whether to draw a line but where. A useful guide is the distinction between disagreement and harm: views, beliefs and ways of life that others find offensive fall within the zone of tolerance; conduct that injures others or denies them the same freedom does not.

The distinction is not always easy to apply, and reasonable people will disagree about particular cases. But it reminds us that the purpose of tolerance is not indifference. It is a way of living together that takes our disagreements seriously enough to leave them unresolved by force.

subject: English
q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Groundwater is a valuable but over-used resource whose depletion often goes unnoticed
Rivers matter more than aquifers for agriculture
Groundwater is always cleaner than surface water
Farmers should stop using pumps altogether
explanation: The passage explains groundwater’s value, shows that it is being pumped faster than it is replenished, and stresses that the damage is hidden until it is severe.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, how are aquifers mainly replenished?
o: By seawater drawn in along the coast
By water pumped back from farms
By rain and river water seeping down through the soil
By melting underground ice
explanation: The second paragraph says aquifers are replenished slowly, ‘mainly by rain and river water seeping down through the soil’; seawater intrusion is described as damage, not recharge.

subject: English
q: Which of the following does the passage give as a consequence of excessive pumping in coastal areas?
o: Rivers overflowing in the dry season
Seawater entering aquifers and making the water salty
Farmers switching to less powerful pumps
Canals delivering more water to farms
explanation: The third paragraph states that ‘in coastal areas, excessive pumping can draw seawater into aquifers and make the water salty’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘inexhaustible’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: impossible to measure
unable to be seen
very costly to obtain
incapable of being used up
explanation: The author warns that an ‘invisible’ resource is not an ‘inexhaustible’ one — being hidden does not mean it can never run out.

subject: English
q: The observation that one farmer’s restraint ‘benefits all his neighbours, while his own pumping costs him little in the short run’ suggests that:
o: farmers deliberately set out to harm their neighbours
individual farmers have little incentive to limit their own pumping
pumping groundwater costs nothing at all
neighbouring farmers usually share a single pump
explanation: If the gains from restraint are spread among neighbours while the cost of pumping falls lightly on oneself, each farmer acting on his own interest will keep pumping; hence the need for collective measures.

subject: English
q: The author’s main purpose in the final paragraph is to:
o: describe how aquifers are formed
blame farmers for the water crisis
argue that cities should stop using groundwater
explain why groundwater is hard to manage and suggest possible measures
explanation: The paragraph states that groundwater is difficult to manage ‘because it is shared and hidden’ and then lists measures such as metering, pricing electricity and recharge.

subject: English
q: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
o: Sleep as Part of Learning
Why the Brain Switches Off at Night
The Dangers of Examinations
Music and Memory
explanation: The passage argues that sleep strengthens newly formed memories and should be treated ‘as part of the work itself’ of learning; it rejects the idea that the mind switches off.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, people who sleep after learning a task often:
o: forget it faster than those who stayed awake
need less effort to learn it in the first place
perform it better the next day than those who stayed awake
remember the details but miss the general pattern
explanation: The second paragraph says such people ‘often perform it better the next day’ and seem better able to draw general patterns from examples.

subject: English
q: The word ‘durable’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: quickly acquired
difficult
long-lasting
impressive
explanation: Study spread over several days with sleep produces ‘more durable results’ — learning that lasts, in contrast to cramming that is quickly lost.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred that the author regards staying up all night before an examination as:
o: counter-productive, because it undermines both memory and concentration
the most efficient way to prepare
harmful only to students who are already unwell
acceptable for students who have studied hard all year
explanation: The author says the practice ‘may feel productive’ but deprives the brain of the process that fixes memories and leaves the student less able to concentrate.

subject: English
q: Why does the author say that sleep is not a substitute for effort?
o: Too much sleep weakens the memory
Sleep helps only with learning music
Examinations test concentration rather than memory
The brain can consolidate only what has already been learned
explanation: The last paragraph explains that ‘the brain can only consolidate what has been learned in the first place’; sleep cannot supply knowledge never acquired.

subject: English
q: By describing sleep ‘not as an indulgence to be sacrificed when work presses, but as part of the work itself’, the author wants readers to:
o: work fewer hours so that they can sleep more
treat adequate sleep as a necessary element of effective study
sleep only after all their work is finished
regard rest as a reward for hard work
explanation: The author rejects seeing sleep as a luxury or reward (an ‘indulgence’) and presents it as contributing directly to learning, so it belongs within study itself.

subject: English
q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: The extended family is being reorganised by changing circumstances, with consequences for public policy
Young people no longer care about their parents
Migration to cities should be discouraged
The extended household has disappeared from South Asia
explanation: The passage traces how migration, housing and women’s work are reshaping the extended household into a dispersed network, and ends with the resulting welfare questions for the state.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, what is the most powerful force changing the extended household?
o: A decline in religious belief
Government policy
Migration
Falling incomes in villages
explanation: The second paragraph opens, ‘The most powerful force is migration’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, what makes it difficult to keep a large family together in the city?
o: Laws limiting the size of households
Small flats and high rents
A shortage of schools
The lack of public transport
explanation: The second paragraph states that ‘in the city, small flats and high rents make it difficult to accommodate a large family even where there is a wish to do so’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘dissolved’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: mixed with water
renewed
officially registered
broken up
explanation: The family is ‘being reorganised rather than dissolved’ — it is changing shape, not breaking up or ceasing to exist.

subject: English
q: The author mentions remittances, visits for weddings and frequent calls to parents in order to:
o: prove that migrants are richer than villagers
show that family ties remain strong despite physical separation
argue that migration should be encouraged
suggest that technology has replaced family visits
explanation: These examples support the claim that ‘it would be wrong to conclude that family ties have weakened in proportion’ to the break-up of the single household.

subject: English
q: The author’s approach to the changes in family life is best described as:
o: nostalgic, mourning the loss of traditional values
celebratory, welcoming the end of the joint family
alarmist, predicting the collapse of society
analytical, explaining causes and consequences without lamenting the change
explanation: The author attributes the change to circumstances rather than declining values, notes that ties persist, and calmly identifies the policy questions that follow.

subject: English
q: The passage is mainly concerned with:
o: the nature of tolerance, the reasons for it and its proper limits
the history of religious persecution
the importance of approving of other people’s choices
the reasons why majorities are usually right
explanation: The passage defines tolerance, gives three reasons for practising it, and then argues that it must stop at conduct that harms others.

subject: English
q: According to the author, tolerance begins only where there is:
o: approval
indifference
disapproval
agreement
explanation: The first paragraph states that ‘tolerance begins only where there is disapproval’; what we like we simply enjoy.

subject: English
q: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons for tolerance given in the passage?
o: Majority opinions have often later been judged mistaken
Adults are entitled to reach their own conclusions about how to live
Tolerance ensures that everyone will eventually agree
Imposed uniformity tends to breed resentment
explanation: The second paragraph gives humility, respect for persons and a prudential reason; nowhere does it claim tolerance leads to agreement — the last paragraph says disagreements are left unresolved.

subject: English
q: The word ‘prudential’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: based on practical good sense and self-interest
based on religious duty
based on legal requirement
based on emotional sympathy
explanation: The ‘prudential’ reason is a practical one: imposing uniformity buys only a short-lived peace at the price of resentment, so tolerance is simply the wiser course.

subject: English
q: On the basis of the distinction drawn in the passage, which of the following would fall outside the zone of tolerance?
o: Holding religious beliefs that most people find strange
Publishing an opinion that many readers find offensive
Choosing an unconventional way of life
Using threats to stop a neighbour from practising his faith
explanation: The author places offensive views, beliefs and ways of life inside the zone of tolerance, but excludes conduct that ‘injures others or denies them the same freedom’, which threatening a neighbour does.

subject: English
q: With which statement would the author most probably agree?
o: Tolerance means having no opinions about how others live
Tolerance means taking disagreements seriously rather than ignoring them
Offensive views should be suppressed by law
A tolerant society must permit every kind of conduct
explanation: The final paragraph says tolerance is ‘not indifference’ but a way of living together that takes disagreements seriously while refusing to settle them by force.
